title: Gestational diabetes
description: Gestational diabetes is a fairly common disorder that typically resolves after childbirth.

contentSections.title: How is gestational diabetes detected?
contentSections.content:
Gestational diabetes is diagnosed through routine blood screening. One example is an Hb1Ac test before week 20 to check for undiagnosed diabetes or any risk of developing it later.

If your result is at least 42 mmol/mol, you will be referred to a diabetes in pregnancy service.

contentSections.title: What causes gestational diabetes?
contentSections.content:
Gestational diabetes develops as a result of increasing glucose levels in the mother's blood after about 24 weeks of pregnancy.

This is due to two factors. Firstly, the human body needs four times more insulin than normal to supply energy to both mum and pēpi. Secondly, hormones in the placenta (e.g. cortisol and human placental lactogen) block the body's insulin, which raises the glucose levels.

contentSections.title: What does this mean for my pregnancy care?
contentSections.content:
Potential complications include birthing difficulties related to the pēpi over growing in size, and the pēpi experiencing increased health risks related to low calcium and glucose levels after birth. Both mother and pēpi are more likely to develop Type 2 diabetes later in life, so it is recommended that both have yearly GP check-ins.

With informed changes in diet and exercise during pregnancy, gestational diabetes is manageable and typically resolves after childbirth.
